title: Redwood discovery: reliability & incident tolerance with Aurora Systems
summary: Exploratory discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and routing/fallback strategies for Aurora's payment fraud detection inference path. Key concerns: SLOs, multi-region failover, deterministic fallbacks to smaller models, data residency/SOC2, and pricing impact of Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private. Agreed next steps: share latency matrix by region, pricing for Dedicated with reserve burst, security docs, and schedule a technical deep dive / perf run in test env.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Jamie Lin - Send region latency matrix, pricing options for Dedicated and Hosted - due 2026-03-06
Carlos Mendez - Prepare suggested fallback policy template and canary rollout plan - due 2026-03-09
Evelyn Park - Share list of security & compliance questions in CRM thread - due 2026-03-05
Schedule technical deep dive + perf run (SE-led) for week of 2026-03-16
action_items: Jamie Lin: Email Aurora latency/throughput spreadsheet and Dedicated pricing (includes burst) - due 2026-03-06
Carlos Mendez: Draft fallback policy (primary hosted model -> reduced-size quantized variant -> cached responses on failure) and share examples - due 2026-03-09
Aurora (Priya): Provide expected TPS and 99th pct latency SLOs for production inference - due 2026-03-10
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Lin: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jamie from Redwood, AE for Aurora. We've got Carlos, our SE, on the line. Quick intros?
[00:12] Priya Shah: Hi I'm Priya, head of ML at Aurora, we own the fraud models. Marcus is our infra lead, Evelyn handles security, and Samir product.
[00:20] Carlos Mendez: Hi all, Carlos SE at Redwood, I work on deployments and performance.
[00:25] Marcus O'Neill: Marcus, platform eng, we run k8s across two cloud regions.
[00:30] Jamie Lin: Great. Purpose of this call is to understand your reliability and incident tolerance needs — multi-region routing, fallbacks, SLA expectations — and where Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit.
[00:44] Priya Shah: Yep, the short story: our fraud inference is latency-sensitive, 95th and 99th are critical. If a primary model goes flaky or a region degrades, we need deterministic fallbacks, and we need failover within seconds to a second-tier path. Also data can't leave EMEA for some customers.
[01:02] Carlos Mendez: Understood. Do you have concrete SLO numbers you target?
[01:06] Priya Shah: At a minimum 95th < 150ms for single-request paths, 99th < 400ms ideally. Throughput varies but peak transactions 1200 TPS across EU region, spiky.
[01:18] Marcus O'Neill: And we can't afford a long cold-start during failover; any fallback has to be warm or cached.
[01:25] Jamie Lin: Perfect. Quick high-level: Hosted gives you our public API with managed multi-region routing and built-in fallbacks; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and optional private networking; Private is customer-managed in VPC/on-prem for strict residency. All can do model variants for fallbacks, but operational tradeoffs differ.
[01:45] Samir Rao: What's the typical fallback chain people implement? Primary big model -> smaller model -> cached response?
[01:52] Carlos Mendez: Exactly. A common pattern is: 1) try primary, 2) on error or high latency route to a quantized lower-capacity model variant, 3) finally serve a cached response or a deterministic degraded answer. We call out thresholds for latency and error rates.
[02:07] Evelyn Park: On security, for Hosted, how do you ensure auditability and KMS separation? We need SOC2, and keys in our KMS ideally.
[02:16] Jamie Lin: Hosted is SOC2 compliant and supports customer-managed keys via KMS integrations for Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and audit logs; Dedicated and Private support full KMS/HSM integration and more strict network isolation.
[02:31] Marcus O'Neill: If we pick Hosted with multi-region, how fast is cross-region routing? If eu-west is degraded will traffic go to eu-central or to US? Latency and data residency matter.
[02:40] Carlos Mendez: Routing policy is configurable. By default we route to nearest healthy region with affinity; you can pin to region, prefer local, or define a policy to failover to a secondary region. We can also do split by customer segment. For data residency we can restrict fallback to only allowed regions.
[02:58] Priya Shah: Good — we need those guardrails. For 99th pctl spikes, what's the expected failover time? Seconds, tens of seconds?
[03:06] Carlos Mendez: If you have healthy capacity in secondary endpoints and warm instances, failover can be sub-5s. If instances need to spin up cold, that adds tens of seconds or a couple minutes. That's where Dedicated reserved pools or pre-warmed capacity help.
[03:19] Marcus O'Neill: So Dedicated gives predictable pre-warmed GPUs; Hosted could do burst but is less deterministic?
[03:25] Jamie Lin: Hosted supports burst capacity and auto-scaling, but Dedicated is the path to strict throughput guarantees and lower variability, plus SLA options you can buy into. We can also do hybrid: Dedicated in-region with Hosted as global fallback.
[03:38] Samir Rao: Price delta? Ballpark impact when you need pre-warmed Dedicated vs Hosted pay-as-you-go.
[03:43] Jamie Lin: Pricing varies with instance and commit. Dedicated is committed monthly and tends to lower per-token cost at scale because of reserved capacity; Hosted is pay-as-you-go with slightly higher unit cost but no upfront commitment. We'll send a region-specific pricing matrix.
[03:57] Priya Shah: On model fallbacks, does Redwood support automatic KV caching and prefix caching? We want short-circuit for repetitive checks to save tokens.
[04:05] Carlos Mendez: Yes, Redwood runtime supports KV/prefix caching and can apply TTLs; it can serve cached for identical prompts. That fits into fallback chain as a last-resort fast path with near-zero compute.
[04:16] Evelyn Park: For audits we need immutable logs of inference requests and model version used; can you store or stream these to our SIEM?
[04:24] Jamie Lin: Absolutely. We provide request-level logs, model version tags, and can stream to customers' logging endpoints — S3, SIEM, or Splunk. For Private and Dedicated we can offer longer retention and custom export.
[04:36] Marcus O'Neill: Is there support for canary or A/B rollouts to validate fallback policies before full cutover?
[04:43] Carlos Mendez: Yes, rollout primitives include canaries, percent-based traffic split, and automatic rollback based on error/latency thresholds. You can attach metrics to a rollout.
[04:52] Priya Shah: We want to test an auto-failover where if 99th crosses 450ms, 20% traffic moves to quantized model for 5 minutes and we monitor quality. Can Redwood do that?
[05:01] Carlos Mendez: Yes — you can define SLO-driven routing rules. We'll provide a sample policy.
[05:07] Samir Rao: Any limitations on model architecture for quantized fallbacks? We use custom transformer stacks.
[05:12] Carlos Mendez: We support most open transformer families; quantization support depends on the model compilation path. Some very new architectures may need extra validation; we'll do model onboarding analysis as part of a POC.
[05:25] Jamie Lin: Let's talk SLA numbers — customers typically want 99.9% uptime or better for inference API. For Hosted we publish region-level uptime and we have paid SLAs for Dedicated. Private SLAs depend on deployment. What SLOs are you expecting in contract?
[05:39] Priya Shah: We want an uptime SLA at 99.95 for production inference endpoints, and SLOs for latency at 95th and 99th. If those are not met we need credits and a defined incident timeline.
[05:50] Jamie Lin: For Dedicated we can put 99.95 SLA and compensating credits; for Hosted we offer strong targets and enterprise SLA add-on as part of committed tier. Private tends to be governed by the customer's infra SLA, we can provide operational runbooks.
[06:05] Evelyn Park: Incident management: how fast do you commit to incident responses? Pager coverage?
[06:10] Carlos Mendez: For enterprise customers we offer 24/7 incident response with defined severity levels; P1 response time within 30 minutes for Dedicated enterprise customers. We'll include our incident playbook.
[06:20] Marcus O'Neill: One concern: cross-region failover could increase error surface due to model weights differences or different quantization — could lead to inconsistency in decisions. How do we mitigate that?
[06:31] Carlos Mendez: Great point. Best practice is to keep same model family and a version sync across regions, or run a slightly smaller model compiled to be behaviorally close. We also recommend shadow testing and quality-alerting tied to eval prompt sets so you catch regressions quickly.
[06:45] Priya Shah: For POC we want to run load tests from EU and simulate region outage and measure the end-to-end time to recovery and quality degradation.
[06:52] Jamie Lin: That's standard. We can run a perf harness in our staging with your model, or you can run client-side with our SDK and we'll provide scripts.
[07:00] Samir Rao: On data residency: if fallback goes to another region, can we ensure only metadata is transferred and not PII?
[07:07] Carlos Mendez: Yes — routing policies can be configured to restrict where raw payloads go. You can also apply transformations or tokenization at the edge before sending to Redwood. For Private deployment we keep all data inside your VPC.
[07:18] Priya Shah: If we opt for Dedicated in a EU region and Hosted as global fallback, do we get separate billing buckets? We need cost attribution per team.
[07:25] Jamie Lin: Yes, we can provide per-route and per-token cost breakdowns in Redwood Console and token-level logs for billing alignment.
[07:34] Marcus O'Neill: Any gotchas on warm vs cold startup with GPU backends? We saw cold starts cause 2-3s spikes in other systems.
[07:40] Carlos Mendez: Cold starts depend on model size and infra. With Dedicated reserved pools you get pre-warmed instances and near-zero cold-starts. Hosted can provision warm pools for you with a small reservation or concurrency keep-alive.
[07:52] Evelyn Park: For compliance we'll need SOC/ISO docs and penetration test summary — can you share that?
[07:57] Jamie Lin: Yes, we'll share our security pack. I'll attach SOC2 reports, network diagrams, and data flow details.
[08:05] Priya Shah: Okay, sounds promising. Final question: in a severe region outage, what's the recommended policy to preserve correctness while preserving throughput? Prefer fallback to a smaller model or keep requests queued?
[08:16] Carlos Mendez: We typically recommend: 1) if correctness is paramount, queue or slow down and use retries with backoff; 2) if availability is paramount, route to lower-fidelity quantized model but add a signal in response indicating degraded confidence so downstream can treat accordingly. You can also use hybrid: degrade for low-risk traffic and queue high-risk flows.
[08:36] Samir Rao: That response flagging is helpful for product.
[08:40] Jamie Lin: Great. To recap — we'll send pricing and region latency matrix, security docs, and a suggested fallback policy for your review. Carlos will draft canary/rollout templates and we'll schedule the perf POC for week of 3/16. Aurora to share exact SLO targets and traffic profile.
[08:57] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks.
[09:00] Jamie Lin: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in CRM thread.
[09:03] (call ends)
